locations.name: Fort Churchill (HBC)
locations.description: The successor post to Prince of Wales Fort, established after the French destruction in 1782. It became the main HBC post on the Churchill River and a key base for Arctic exploration and trade.
locations.historicalNotes: Built to replace the destroyed Prince of Wales Fort. Less elaborate than its predecessor. Served as base for Arctic trade and exploration until 1930s. The modern town of Churchill grew up around it.

locations.name: Fort Edmonton
locations.description: Major HBC post that grew to become Alberta's capital. Name means 'beaver hills house' in Cree.
locations.historicalNotes: Originally Fort Augustus (NWC) and Edmonton House (HBC) built side by side. Center of prairie fur trade.
locations.galleryImages: [{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhasls40026m2zhpi43jsew/gallery-0.jpg","caption":"Historic plan-view watercolor of Fort Edmonton","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Wikimedia Commons / historical watercolor / Wikimedia Commons (historical archival image; see file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhasls40026m2zhpi43jsew/gallery-1.jpg","caption":"Strong historical view tied to the fort era","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Wikimedia Commons / historical image / Wikimedia Commons (historical archival image; see file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhasls40026m2zhpi43jsew/gallery-2.jpg","caption":"High-resolution historical image from a U.S. archival source via Commons","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons / Wikimedia Commons (historical archival image; see file page)"}]

locations.name: Fort Edmonton (HBC)
locations.description: The main HBC post on the upper North Saskatchewan River, serving as the gateway to the Athabasca country and the mountain passes to the Pacific. It was one of the most important posts in the entire HBC network.
locations.historicalNotes: Built 1795 to compete with NWC's Fort Augustus across the river. Relocated several times. Chief Factor John Rowand made it the dominant post in the region (1823-1854). Supplied provisions for the entire Saskatchewan district. The city of Edmonton grew from it.

locations.name: Fort Garry
locations.description: Hudson's Bay Company fort at the junction of the Red and Assiniboine Rivers. Nucleus of modern Winnipeg.
locations.historicalNotes: Center of the Red River Settlement and later the provisional government during the 1869 Red River Resistance.

locations.name: Fort Garry (Upper)
locations.description: The main HBC post at the Forks of the Red and Assiniboine Rivers, which became the center of the Red River Settlement and eventually the city of Winnipeg. It was the gateway to the western plains.
locations.historicalNotes: Built after the 1821 merger to replace Fort Gibraltar. Named for Nicholas Garry, HBC deputy governor. Seat of government for Rupert's Land. Louis Riel seized it in 1869-1870 during the Red River Rebellion. Site now in downtown Winnipeg.
locations.galleryImages: [{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxl6000jm2a3g5tcl5vu/gallery-0.jpg","caption":"Current high-resolution image of the surviving gate area","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Own work on Wikimedia Commons / Wikimedia Commons (free-license file; see file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxl6000jm2a3g5tcl5vu/gallery-1.jpg","caption":"Clear gate view useful in-app as a modern site marker","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Wikimedia Commons site photograph / Wikimedia Commons (free-license file; see file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxl6000jm2a3g5tcl5vu/gallery-2.jpg","caption":"Interpretive park view tied to the site","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Wikimedia Commons site photograph / Wikimedia Commons (free-license file; see file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxl6000jm2a3g5tcl5vu/gallery-3.jpg","caption":"Upper Fort Garry Gate, Winnipeg — the only surviving structure of Upper Fort Garry","credit":"Wikimedia Commons"}]

locations.name: Fort William
locations.description: The grand depot of the North West Company, where voyageurs from Montreal met winterers from the interior.
locations.historicalNotes: Named after William McGillivray. Site of the annual Rendezvous where up to 2,000 people gathered.
locations.galleryImages: [{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhbjrr2000vm2mb4xb3au6o/gallery-0.jpg","caption":"Historic watercolor of the North West Company establishment","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Library and Archives Canada via Commons / Public Domain Mark / PD-Art (Commons file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhbjrr2000vm2mb4xb3au6o/gallery-1.jpg","caption":"Good architectural/site detail for app use","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Own work on Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 / GFDL (Commons file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhbjrr2000vm2mb4xb3au6o/gallery-2.jpg","caption":"Fort William Historical Park view","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Own work on Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 / GFDL (Commons file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhbjrr2000vm2mb4xb3au6o/gallery-3.jpg","caption":"","credit":""},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhbjrr2000vm2mb4xb3au6o/gallery-4.jpg","caption":"Historic streetscape of Fort William, circa 1920","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Archives of Ontario via Commons / Open Government Licence - Ontario"}]

locations.name: Fort William (NWC)
locations.description: The great inland headquarters of the North West Company on Lake Superior. Every summer, the partners from Montreal and the wintering partners from the interior met here for the annual rendezvous to exchange furs, trade goods, and conduct company business.
locations.historicalNotes: Replaced Grand Portage after it fell into US territory (1796). Named for William McGillivray, NWC chief director. At its peak, over 2,000 people gathered for the annual meeting. Seized by Lord Selkirk (1816) during the pemmican war. Passed to HBC 1821. Reconstructed as a major heritage site.
locations.galleryImages: [{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxn40015m2a37q2atmqk/gallery-0.jpg","caption":"","credit":""},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxn40015m2a37q2atmqk/gallery-1.jpg","caption":"Reconstructed buildings linked to the NWC fort","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Own work on Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 / GFDL (Commons file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxn40015m2a37q2atmqk/gallery-2.jpg","caption":"Fort William Historical Park","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Own work on Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 / GFDL (Commons file page)"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxn40015m2a37q2atmqk/gallery-3.jpg","caption":"Modern reconstructed site tied to the NWC post","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Own work on Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 (Commons file page)"}]

locations.name: Rocky Mountain House
locations.description: The westernmost HBC post in the Saskatchewan district, located near the Rocky Mountains. It served as a base for trade with the Blackfoot Confederacy and for exploration of the mountain passes.
locations.historicalNotes: Built near NWC's Rocky Mountain House. David Thompson used it as base for his 1807 crossing of the Rockies. Dangerous location due to Blackfoot raids. Abandoned and rebuilt multiple times. Now a National Historic Site.
locations.galleryImages: [{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxka000dm2a38u2u5e1v/gallery-0.jpg","caption":"Wide historic-site view","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Commons site photograph / Creative Commons license on Commons file page"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxka000dm2a38u2u5e1v/gallery-1.jpg","caption":"Modern settlement view for place context","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Commons site photograph / Creative Commons license on Commons file page"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxka000dm2a38u2u5e1v/gallery-2.jpg","caption":"","credit":""},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxka000dm2a38u2u5e1v/gallery-3.jpg","caption":"Rocky Mountain House National Historic Site, Alberta","credit":"Wikimedia Commons"}]

locations.name: Rocky Mountain House (NWC)
locations.description: A North West Company post near the Rocky Mountains, built close to the HBC's Acton House. David Thompson used it as a base for his exploration of the mountain passes and the Columbia River.
locations.historicalNotes: Built same time as HBC's nearby post. David Thompson's base for his 1807 crossing of the Rockies via Howse Pass. Later moved several times. Site now a National Historic Site shared with HBC remains.
locations.galleryImages: [{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxoe001pm2a35trj97gi/gallery-1.jpg","caption":"Historic-site landscape linked to the NWC establishment","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Commons site photograph / Creative Commons license on Commons file page"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxoe001pm2a35trj97gi/gallery-2.jpg","caption":"Additional direct site view","credit":"Wikimedia Commons / Commons site photograph / Creative Commons license on Commons file page"},{"url":"https://pub-376806a1556549999cfff53a786882dd.r2.dev/locations/cmlhcpxoe001pm2a35trj97gi/gallery-3.jpg","caption":"","credit":""}]

locations.name: Upper Fort Garry
locations.description: The main Hudson's Bay Company fort at the junction of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, which became the nucleus of modern Winnipeg.
locations.historicalNotes: Upper Fort Garry was the center of the Red River Settlement and later the site of Louis Riel's provisional government during the Red River Resistance of 1869-70. Most of the fort was demolished in the 1880s, but the Governor's Gate survives in downtown Winnipeg. The Forks, where the rivers meet, was a gathering place for 6,000 years before European contact.
